title: Love made visible
hookLine: Gibran: work is love made visible (The Prophet, 1923)

cards: A ship is waiting in the harbor to take a man home after years away. Before he boards, the people of the city gather around him and, one by one, ask him to speak. About love.
About marriage. About children. Later a farmer, a ploughman, steps forward and asks him to speak of work.
That's a scene from The Prophet, a book by the Lebanese American poet Kahlil Gibran. The man is Almustafa, and inside his long answer about work sit five words: "Work is love made visible."
Today's word is the one who said it: Almustafa.

teach.b: First, the claim itself. Love, on its own, can't be seen; you can't photograph it. But a meal can be seen.
A mended coat. A swept step. In Almustafa's answer, work is where love leaves the inside of a person and becomes something you can touch.

teach.h: AS IF THE BELOVED WOULD WEAR IT.
teach.b: Second, what working with love looks like, in paraphrase: weaving cloth with threads drawn from your own heart, as if someone you love would wear it. Building a house as if your beloved would live in it.
Sowing seeds with tenderness, as if the one you love would eat the harvest. The test is simple: who is this for, in your mind, while you make it? Third, the hard half.

Almustafa warns, again in paraphrase, that bread baked with indifference is bitter bread, and feeds only half of a person's hunger. Grudge the crushing of the grapes, he says, and the grudge becomes a poison in the wine.
The same loaf, two different breads.
Fourth, how this gathers up the days just before it. Ihsan asked for excellence, as though seen. Qing forgot the prize.
Ruskin wanted joy in the making. Morris wanted hope in it. Gibran names what might be underneath all of them: the person you're doing it for.
It doesn't have to be grand. A shirt ironed for a parent's interview. A gate fixed before a neighbor gets home.
Seen this way, an ordinary chore is a small, visible message, even if nobody ever reads it as one.

how: Readers of The Prophet, including some people who keep a spiritual life outside any one tradition, return to its chapter on work when they think about their own work.

s: in The Prophet, a ploughman asks Almustafa to speak of work
his answer ends with "work is love made visible."
Almustafa says any work, done any way, is equally good
he warns that bread baked with indifference is bitter.
the image for working with love is weaving cloth as if the beloved would wear it
he also speaks of building a house and sowing seeds the same way.

games.q: you're baking bread, but your mind is elsewhere and you resent the chore. what does Almustafa say about that loaf?
o: bread is bread; it feeds the same.
it's bitter bread, feeding only half a hunger.
it's fine as long as it looks good.
games.why: he says bread baked with indifference is bitter and feeds only half of a person's hunger.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love, and let their face come clear.

Think of one small job you could do for them, folding their laundry, cooking the dish they like, and picture doing it slowly with them in mind the whole time, the way Almustafa describes weaving cloth for the beloved.
If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Almustafa. The speaker in Gibran's The Prophet who tells the ploughman that work is love made visible. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a small, visible message. Who is it for? That's day nine hundred six.
